## Your risks

What could reach a household like yours in Fort Bend County, Texas over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first.

### What to know and do

#### 1. Heat wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in a ten-year stretch around 2050 (about 1.5 times a year).[6, 21]

**Includes:** a blackout during a heat wave.

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[22] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[23] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[23] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[22] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[24]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[22] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[23] Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot, red skin that may be dry or damp, a fast, strong pulse, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler, cool them with cool cloths or a cool bath, and give them nothing to drink.[25]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 2. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.4 times a year).[26]

**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[27] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[28] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[29] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[30] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[31]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[32] Do not use expired medicines.[33]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 3. Hurricane

Of 100 households like yours, about 60 (38–81) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[10, 11, 12, 14]

**Includes:** inland flooding from a tropical storm.

**What helps.** Know your evacuation zone, your routes and where you would stay. If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and officials tell you to leave, go right away.[3] If you are not told to leave, shelter from the wind in a small inside room, closet or hallway away from windows, on the lowest floor that will not flood.[3, 34] Clear drains and gutters, bring in outdoor furniture, and think about storm shutters. Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[3] A flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start, so buy it well before a storm.[35] If you would leave in an electric car, keep it fully charged all hurricane season.[36]

**What to avoid.** Never walk or drive through floodwater. One foot of moving water can sweep a car away.[35] Do not drive or charge an electric car that has been in floodwater. Salt water can start a battery fire.[36] Never run a generator inside your home or garage.[37]

**How bad:** Serious (mostly data).

#### 4. Cold wave

Of 100 households like yours, about 28 will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years.[21]

**Includes:** rolling blackouts in extreme cold.

**What helps.** Keep extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats, and pick one room to keep warm.[38] If you cannot keep your home warm, go to a warming center. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[39] Learn how to keep pipes from freezing, and test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before winter.[40] Keep a car kit with jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, water and snacks, and keep the gas tank full.[40] Check on older neighbours often.[38] Know the signs of hypothermia, such as shivering, confusion and slurred speech. A body temperature below 95°F is an emergency. Warm the center of the body first.[40]

**What to avoid.** Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Use generators and grills only outdoors, away from windows.[40] Choose electric space heaters with automatic shut-off, and keep them 3 feet from anything that can burn.[38, 41] Do not overdo it when you shovel snow.[40]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 5. Burst pipe or water leak

Of 100 households like yours, about 14 will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[42]

**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[43, 44] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[43] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[44] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[43]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[44] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[43]

**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

#### 6. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain

Of 100 households like yours, about 4 (1–9) will have flood water reach their home in a ten-year stretch around 2050.[6, 13, 14]

**Includes:** flash flood; basement or street flooding in heavy rain.

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[35] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[35] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[45] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[35]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[35] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[46] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[35] Leave if you are told to.[47]

**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

#### 7. House fire

Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.[17]

**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[48] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[49] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[49] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[49] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[49] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[50]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[49] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[49] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[49]

**How bad:** Severe (based on data).

#### 8. Tornado

Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 4) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.[10, 14]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[51] The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[51, 52] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[51] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. In your shelter, protect your head and neck with your arms, and pile blankets or cushions around you.[51] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[53]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[51] There is no safe place in a car during a tornado, only less dangerous ones. If you are caught, stay buckled in and keep your head below the windows.[51] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[53]

**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

## Your targets

How long to be ready for each kind of disruption at the 1-in-50 setting. That is why the plan also gives you ways to cope when a target runs out.[14, 97]

| No grid power at home | about 5 days (up to 7 days) | about 3 days | about 9 days | two weeks |
| Tap water must be treated | about 5 days (1 day to 2 weeks) | not known | worst on record: about 6 days | two weeks |
| No tap water at all | about 2 days (up to 7 days) | not known | not known | three days |
| Can't get to a store | about 10 days (7 days to 3 weeks) | not known | not known | two weeks |
| Dangerous heat or cold indoors | about 3 days (up to 5 days) | about 3 days | about 9 days | three days |
| Medication and medical-supply continuity | about 3 weeks (2 weeks to 1½ months) | not known | not known | one month |
| No phone, internet or card payments | about 2 days (up to 5 days) | not known | not known | three days |

Brackets show how uncertain a target is. "Not known": no restoration records for the event behind that target; "worst on record": no such records either, so the worst event on record stands in (named below).

**How well do these numbers hold up?** Tested against 22 real disasters, this version covered 6, partly covered 9, fell short on 6 and could not model 1.[98] Treat each target as a floor, not a promise. If your area has lived through something longer, plan for that.

### No grid power at home: about 5 days (up to 7 days)

**What helps.** A light for each person, a radio and phone power are in your plan; keeping food cold and charging up are on the forecast list; registries are under Local help.

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[37] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[99] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911.[100] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[99] Treat every downed power line as live: stay at least 30 feet from it and anything it touches, and call 911.[101] If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.[102]

The worst power cut in your region's records (where it was worst, about 120 miles (193 km) away) was Hurricane Harvey (2017); being ready for 5 days would have left some homes that lost power still waiting (about 50 in 100 of all customers there were still out).[10, 11, 12, 14, 21, 94, 103, 104]

### Tap water must be treated: about 5 days (1 day to 2 weeks)

**What helps.** Use bottled water, or bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute. Boil for three minutes above 5,000 feet, then let it cool.[105] If you cannot boil water, add plain unscented bleach: 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon. Stir, and wait 30 minutes.[105] Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, baby formula and ice. If the power is out too, a camp stove works, but only outdoors.[37]

**What to avoid.** Do not use water or ice from the fridge dispenser while a notice is on. Boil tap water even if it went through a home filter or a filter pitcher.[106] Boiling does not help if the notice warns of chemicals. That is a do-not-drink notice, and you need stored or bottled water instead.[106, 107]

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[113] You can pick a level in the plan. **What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[113] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[118] Never drink pool or spa water. ## Your shelter plan

Pick a spot for each danger below, at home and at work, and practice going there.[4]

**Strong wind.** In a high wind or severe thunderstorm warning, go inside a sturdy building, to an inside room or basement.[139] Stay away from windows while damaging wind is near.[140]

**Tornado.** A safe room or storm shelter is best; next is a small inside room with no windows on the lowest floor.[51] Even a tied-down mobile home is not safe.[52]

**Hurricane.** If officials tell your evacuation zone to leave, go right away. If you stay, use an inside room away from windows.[3]

**Chemical release.** If told to stay inside, go to an above-ground room with few openings. Close the windows, doors and vents, turn off fans and air conditioning, and seal the room with plastic sheeting and duct tape.[141]

**Radiation.** If officials warn of fallout, get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Go to a basement or the middle of a brick or concrete building.[86]

## When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast

Hurricanes, winter storms and heat waves usually come with warning. Keep your phone charged when one is forecast, and use the time the same way each time.[3]

**Before any storm**

- Charge phones, power banks and other batteries.[142] 
- Fill the car's tank and get some cash, since card readers and cash machines need power.[142] Charge the power station.[142] If you would leave in an electric car, charge it fully.[36]
- Refill prescriptions if you can.[142]
- Fill the bathtub and other large containers with water for flushing and cleaning.[142]
- Turn the fridge to its coldest setting and keep the doors shut.[142] A full freezer keeps food cold for about 48 hours, a fridge for about four.[99]
- Bring in or tie down outdoor furniture and grills.[3]
- Check your evacuation zone and your plan to leave.[3]
- Check with neighbors, older adults and anyone who may need help.[3]

**Before a hard freeze.** Let hot and cold water drip from a faucet at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher. Make sure everyone knows how to shut off the water in case a pipe bursts.[44]

**Before a heat wave.** Pick a place to cool down, such as a library, or ask your local health department about cooling options. Plan to check on family, older adults and neighbors. Fans do not lower body temperature.[23]

## After a disaster: the first 30 days

**Your county.** Fort Bend County, Texas had 2 federal major-disaster declarations in the last five full years.[167]

Recovery takes weeks. These steps come in rough order.

**Going home.** Go back only when local officials say it is safe. Do not go inside if you smell gas or the building looks damaged.[168] Run a generator only outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[37]

**Insurance and records.** Before you clean up, take photos and videos and make a list of the damage.[168] Keep every receipt.[169] Call your insurer as soon as you can, and an adjuster will come to inspect. Check the adjuster's estimate, and talk to them before you sign a repair contract.[170]

**Help from FEMA.** If a federal disaster declaration covers your county, apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.[171] FEMA help does not replace insurance.[172]

**Scams.** FEMA never charges to apply or to inspect.[173] Its inspectors carry an official photo ID and never ask for your bank details; a FEMA shirt is not an ID.[169] Never sign your insurance check over to a contractor, and walk away from anyone who wants cash up front.[174]

**Medicine.** In a declared disaster, Medicare drug plans can help you find a pharmacy and replace lost medicine.[175] Many states let a pharmacist give an emergency supply when your prescriber cannot be reached, and the rules differ by state.[153] Healthcare Ready's Rx Open map shows which pharmacies are open in a disaster area.[176]

**Papers.** To replace lost IDs, start with your birth certificate, from the vital records office of the state where you were born.[177]
